title: Morning and evening
hook: remember your Lord's name morning and evening, and prostrate at night (76:25–26)

segments.voice: Yesterday: for love of Him, and your line, no thanks wanted. Did someone get fed, and did you let the thanks pass? Today, our last day in al-Insan, and the two hinges of every day. Day six hundred sixty-one.

Every day has two doors. The one you walk out of in the morning, keys in hand, coffee half finished. And the one you walk back through in the evening, shoes off, bag dropped, the day behind you. Most of us cross both without noticing, already thinking about the next thing. Near the end of surah al-Insan, after its long picture of a garden for the grateful, the Qur'an gives the Prophet a short instruction about those two doors.
screen: `OUT IN THE MORNING, IN AT EVENING.`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-five, in Pickthall's translation: "Remember the name of thy Lord at morn and evening." The Arabic is bukratan wa asila. Bukrah is the early morning, the first hours. Asil is the late afternoon into evening, as the light goes gold. Then verse twenty-six: and part of the night, prostrate to Him, and glorify Him through a long night. So the day gets framed. Begin with His name. End with His name. Give some of the dark to prayer. Commentators connect these times to the daily prayers, the dawn prayer, the afternoon and evening prayers, and the night prayer. And the Qur'an uses the same pairing elsewhere: in surah al-Ahzab, believers are told to remember Allah often, and glorify Him morning and evening. From these verses and many hadith grew a whole practice that millions of Muslims keep: the adhkar of the morning and the evening. Short remembrances, said after the dawn prayer and again before or after sunset. There are phrases of praise, verses like Ayat al-Kursi and the last three surahs, and a prayer for forgiveness that a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari calls the master of all prayers for forgiveness, to be said morning and evening. Some people say them from a small booklet; some from memory, walking to the bus. Why the two ends of the day? Because those are the hinges. What you say as the door opens sets the tone for whatever comes through it. And what you say as it closes decides what you carry into sleep. The middle of the day will be busy. The edges can be held.
screen: `BEGIN WITH HIS NAME, END WITH IT.`

segments.voice: The practice: remember morning and evening. Sit, and choose one short line you'll say at both doors of tomorrow. If you pray, it might be bismillah, or subhanallah, or alhamdulillah, or the name of your Lord, said slowly. If you don't, it might be a single breath of thanks. Now picture tomorrow's first door, and say the line there. Then picture tomorrow's last door, and say it again. The bell holds the time.
Morning and evening. In 76:25 the Prophet is told to remember his Lord's name bukratan wa asila, at the two edges of the day, and to give part of the night to prayer. Today's word.
Your line: morning and evening. Tonight, as you come through the last door of the day, say your line once. Tomorrow, say it again on the way out. Day six hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Many Muslims recite the adhkar of the morning and evening, short remembrances, verses and prayers, after the dawn prayer and around sunset, often from a small booklet or from memory, following 76:25, 33:42 and many hadith.

what it means: frame the day with Allah's name at both edges, and give part of the night to prostration.
what a scholar hears: commentators map bukrah and asil onto the dawn, afternoon and evening prayers; the adhkar tradition draws on this and 33:42.
